input: In this section, we take a closer look at the pricing economics of the new SaaS tier, and the picture that emerges is a challenging one. The tier is priced at $64 per unit, while the variable cost associated with each unit is $42 per unit, which means that every unit sold generates a contribution of $22 that can be applied toward the fixed costs of $210k per year. When these figures are combined, the break-even volume works out to 9545 units per year. However, the current volume is just 3983 units per year, which means the tier is operating at a shortfall of 5562 units relative to the break-even point, highlighting the scale of the gap that would need to be closed. It is important to note that the volume figures are last year's actuals, and that the effect of the price on volume has not been estimated at this stage, so any change in price would introduce an additional layer of uncertainty into the analysis, making it difficult to say with confidence how the position might evolve going forward.
target: The SaaS tier does not cover its costs at the current volume. Break-even volume is 9545 units per year, the volume at which the contribution from units sold equals the fixed costs. Last year's volume was 3983 units, a shortfall of 5562 units against break-even. The price is $64 per unit and the variable cost is $42 per unit. Each unit sold contributes $22, and the fixed costs are $210k per year. The contribution is what each unit pays toward the fixed costs after its own variable cost has been met, and the tier covers its costs only when the contributions of all the units sold add up to the fixed-cost figure. At the current volume the contribution covers less than half of the fixed costs; the tier runs at a loss for as long as volume stays at last year's level and the price and costs stay as stated. The gap closes if volume grows at the current price. A higher price or lower costs would also close it arithmetically, but the figures support only the first reading. The volume figures are last year's actuals, and the effect of the price on volume is not estimated. A higher price would change the contribution per unit, and nothing in the figures states what it would do to the volume; the break-even volume is the volume the current price requires, no more.
